response.answer_text: For a red blood cell whose membrane is water permeable but not permeable to the relevant solutes, osmosis moves water according to its concentration gradient across the membrane, which is inversely proportional to the solutes' concentration [ev_006]. In that situation the solute cannot pass through the membrane, but the water can [ev_002].  In an isotonic solution, the extracellular fluid has the same osmolarity as the cell, and there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell [ev_004] [ev_001]; the cell keeps its normal volume and shape [ev_003]. In a hypertonic solution, the surrounding fluid has greater solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes out of the cell into the surrounding fluid and the red blood cell shrivels [ev_004] [ev_003]. In a hypotonic solution, the surrounding fluid has lower solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes into the red blood cell, causing it to swell and possibly rupture (lyse) [ev_004] [ev_003]. Water moves by osmosis, the diffusion of water through a semipermeable membrane, and the membrane limits the solutes' diffusion [ev_006] [ev_008]. Regarding your question: no. 'No net water movement' in an isotonic solution does not mean individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane; the source states there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, although water will still move in and out [ev_004].
